subject: physics_2
question_text: Using dimensional analysis obtain an expression for the speed of transverse waves in a stretched string.

mark_split.label: Dimensional formulas of T and μ

verification.note: The 1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. The two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE for this paper: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers, so neither check was run. Physics hand-checked: [T] = MLT⁻² (a force), [μ] = ML⁻¹ (mass per length), so T/μ has dimensions MLT⁻²/ML⁻¹ = L²T⁻² = [v²]; hence v = K√(T/μ) with K dimensionless. The exact treatment gives K = 1.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order — the two quantities the speed depends on, their dimensional formulas, and the final expression.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Dimensional formulas
steps.mark_note: D.F. of T and μ written
lines: The speed v of a transverse wave on a
stretched string depends on the tension T
in the string and its linear density μ

lines.text: D.F. of μ = M/L = ML⁻¹ ; v = LT⁻¹

steps.margin_note: First mark. Name the two quantities and write both dimensional formulas.
steps.why: Dimensional analysis can only start from a guessed list of quantities. Tension supplies the restoring force and linear density the inertia, so these two are the physical inputs.
common_mistakes: Using density ρ (ML⁻³) instead of linear density μ (ML⁻¹) — a string is measured per unit length, not per unit volume.
Writing the dimensional formula of tension as MLT⁻¹ — tension is a force, MLT⁻².

recall.must_convey: That the speed depends on tension T (dimensions MLT⁻²) and linear density μ (dimensions ML⁻¹).
accept: depends on tension and linear density
mu is mass per unit length, ML inverse
reject: v equals K root T by mu

steps.memory_tip: Force over inertia: tension pulls the string back, linear density slows it down.

steps.label: Combining the dimensions
lines: So v² matches T/μ. Taking the square root:
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Show T/μ = L²T⁻² before writing the root — the division IS the working.
steps.why: Matching dimensions on both sides is the whole method: T/μ is the only combination of the two inputs with the dimensions of speed squared. The dimensionless constant K cannot come from dimensions — the exact derivation gives K = 1.
common_mistakes: Writing v = K(T/μ) without the square root — T/μ has the dimensions of v², not v.
Dropping the constant K. Dimensional analysis can never fix a pure number, so K must be stated.

recall.must_convey: That T/μ has the dimensions of v², so v = K√(T/μ) with K a dimensionless constant.
accept: T by mu gives L squared T minus two
v equals K root T over mu
square root of tension by linear density

steps.memory_tip: T over μ lands on v squared, so the answer always carries a square root.

insider_note: The square root and the stated constant K carry the second mark — v = K(T/μ) without the root is the standard way this answer dies.
